newsitem.title: UK: Policewoman "serious" as N.Irish peace hopes fade.
newsitem.headline: Policewoman "serious" as N.Irish peace hopes fade.

text.p: A 46-year-old Northern Ireland policewoman was seriously ill on Friday after a six-hour operation to remove an IRA sniper's bullet from her chest.
Hospital sources in Londonderry said Alice Collins, a mother of three, was serious but stable after being shot in the back at a security hut outside the city's courthouse on Thursday.

Dick Spring, Ireland's deputy prime minister, echoing widespred British and Irish condemnation, called on the guerrillas to abandon violence and said the shooting further delayed the day when their Sinn Fein political ally would get a place in all-party talks about the province.

The attack dashed media rumours about a possible partial Irish Republican Army truce in the leadup to British and Irish elections and fuelled worries of retaliation on Catholics by Protestant "Loyalist" extremists who support British rule.
"It has now been established that the constable was shot in the back with a high velocity round," Stuart Tosh, the Royal Ulster Constabulary's deputy police commander in Londonderry told BBC radio.
"It is also clear that the coward who carried out the crime must have known that he was firing at a woman whilst her back was turned."
The IRA has intensified a campaign of bomb and gun attacks in Northern Ireland aimed at ending British sovereignty, killing two soldiers since October. It has also set off bombs in mainland Britain.
Britain and Ireland say that Sinn Fein will not be invited to talks until the republican militarists abandon violence.
Media reports on Thursday suggested the IRA would announce a scaling down of hostilities to try to win votes for Sinn Fein which is contesting Northern Ireland seats in the May 1 British election.
Spring, speaking on Irish radio, warned that IRA violence would keep Sinn Fein in a political wilderness no matter what party was in power in Britain.

Challenging Sinn Fein leader Gerry Adams to condemn the attack, Spring said: "His party is still associated with support for what the IRA is doing. Nobody in their right minds will talk to them at the present time while the shooting is continuing.
"If they want to be part of the political process, the shooting must stop, the threat of violence must be removed, and we will all work around the table together."

Adams told BBC radio he "very much regretted" the shooting but refused to condemn it. It and other recent violence would not have happened if Sinn Fein had been given a place in all-party talks, he said.
"I and the Sinn Fein leadership have exerted as much influence as we can at this time to bring about an end to all armed actions."
Billy Hutchinson, a politician close to banned Loyalist guerrillas, urged pro-British Protestant hardliners not to accelerate a slide into worse violence by vengeful attacks on Catholic nationalists.
The Londonderry attack was "a desperate attempt by the IRA to bring Loyalists back into full war. I think Loyalists should resist that," he told Reuters.
Loyalist commanders insist that their October 1994 ceasefire is still in force in spite of two Catholic murders and other attacks in the past year.The IRA draws support in Catholic zones.
